aaqParts.name: Research method
aaqParts.tip: Look for random assignment, manipulation of a variable, and control/experimental groups.
aaqParts.mistake: Calling an experiment a "correlational study" because it measured variables. Random assignment + a manipulated variable = experiment.

aaqParts.name: Research variable
aaqParts.tip: Scan the Method section for how the variable was actually measured or tested.
aaqParts.mistake: Giving a textbook definition instead of how THIS study measured it.

aaqParts.name: Statistic interpretation
aaqParts.tip: Always connect the number back to what it means for the research question.
aaqParts.mistake: Just restating the numbers ("the mean was 7.81") without saying which group did better and what that tells us.

aaqParts.name: Ethical guidelines
aaqParts.tip: Read the Method section carefully. Ethical practices are often described without being named.
aaqParts.mistake: Naming a guideline the researchers SHOULD have followed but that the article never describes.

aaqParts.name: Generalizability
aaqParts.tip: The demographic table is the key. Reference specific percentages from the participant data.
aaqParts.mistake: Saying "the study is (not) generalizable" without citing specific demographics (age, race, gender, location).

aaqParts.name: Argumentation
aaqParts.tip: Use specific numbers from the Results section and explicitly say whether they support or refute the hypothesis.
aaqParts.mistake: A conclusion with no specific data (1 pt), or data with no explanation of how it connects to the hypothesis (1 pt). You need both for 2.

ebqParts.label: A
ebqParts.name: Claim
ebqParts.q: Propose a specific and defensible claim based in psychological science that responds to the question.
ebqParts.tip: Take a clear position the sources can back up. "Should," "because," and "depends on" help make a claim specific.
ebqParts.mistake: A vague claim ("Social media affects teenagers") or one that just restates the question earns 0.

ebqParts.label: B(i)
ebqParts.name: Evidence #1
ebqParts.q: Support your claim using at least one piece of specific and relevant evidence from one of the sources.
ebqParts.tip: Pick specific data (numbers, groups, results) and cite it: "(Source 1)" or "According to Source 1…".
ebqParts.mistake: No citation, or a vague summary of a source instead of specific data.

ebqParts.label: B(ii)
ebqParts.name: Explain + apply
ebqParts.q: Explain how the evidence from Part B(i) supports your claim using a psychological perspective, theory, concept, or research finding learned in AP Psychology.
ebqParts.tip: Two moves: (1) say HOW the evidence supports your claim, (2) name a psych concept from class and use it to explain WHY the result happened.
ebqParts.mistake: Explaining the evidence without applying a concept (1 pt), or "applying" a term that comes from the sources (depression, sleep, screen time…).

ebqParts.label: C(i)
ebqParts.name: Evidence #2
ebqParts.q: Support your claim using an additional piece of specific and relevant evidence from a different source than the one that you used to support your claim in Part B(i).
ebqParts.tip: Use a DIFFERENT source than Part B. Plan which two sources you will use during the reading period.
ebqParts.mistake: Using the same source as Part B(i): it earns 0 even if the evidence is good.

ebqParts.label: C(ii)
ebqParts.name: Explain + apply
ebqParts.q: Explain how the evidence from Part C(i) supports your claim using a different psychological perspective, theory, concept, or research finding learned in AP Psychology than the one that you used in Part B(ii).
ebqParts.tip: Use a DIFFERENT concept than Part B(ii). Plan two concepts before you start writing.
ebqParts.mistake: Reusing the concept from B(ii) caps this part at 1 point.

frq.aaqRubric:
AP Psychology Article Analysis Question (AAQ) rubric. Parts A-E are worth 1 point each; Part F is worth 2 points.
A (Research method, task verb IDENTIFY): earn the point for naming the correct research method (experiment, correlational study, case study, naturalistic observation, meta-analysis, etc.). Random assignment + a manipulated variable = experiment. No explanation is required.
B (Research variable, STATE): earn the point for the operational definition used IN THIS STUDY: how the researchers actually measured or manipulated the variable, with measurable specifics from the Method. A general textbook definition earns 0.
C (Statistic interpretation, DESCRIBE): earn the point for saying what the statistic means for the study (which group did better / direction and meaning of the relationship) and connecting it to what was investigated. Only restating the numbers earns 0.
D (Ethical guidelines, IDENTIFY + DESCRIBE): earn the point only if the student names a specific ethical guideline that the article actually describes AND describes how the researchers applied it, with evidence from the article. A guideline not described in the article earns 0.
E (Generalizability, EXPLAIN): earn the point for a claim about whether the findings generalize, naming a specific population, AND citing specific participant demographics from the study (percentages, ages, location, etc.). No specific demographics = 0.
F (Argumentation, EXPLAIN): point 1 for citing a specific result (data) from the study; point 2 for an accurate explanation of how that result supports or refutes the hypothesis/claim. Claiming a correlational or observational study proves causation is NOT accurate.
Be fair like a real AP reader: accept any correct wording, do not require the model answer's exact words, ignore spelling, and do not award points for vague or incorrect answers.
frq.ebqRubric:
AP Psychology Evidence-Based Question (EBQ) rubric, 7 points.
A (Claim, 1 pt, PROPOSE): a specific, defensible claim based in psychological science that responds to the question. Vague claims ("Social media affects teenagers") or restatements of the question earn 0.
B(i) (Evidence #1, 1 pt, SUPPORT): specific, relevant evidence from ONE source that supports the claim, with a citation such as "(Source 1)" or "According to Source 1". No citation = 0. Vague summaries = 0.
B(ii) (Explain + apply, 2 pts): point 1 for explaining how the B(i) evidence supports the claim; point 2 for ALSO applying a psychological perspective, theory, concept, or research finding learned in AP Psychology (e.g., social comparison theory, operant conditioning, circadian rhythm, memory consolidation, Erikson, Piaget, neuroplasticity, prefrontal cortex). Terms that come from the sources themselves (e.g., depression, well-being, sleep, screen time), "statistically significant," and vague popular ideas do NOT count as applied concepts. Opinion only = 0.
C(i) (Evidence #2, 1 pt): like B(i) but from a DIFFERENT source than B(i). Same source as B(i) = 0.
C(ii) (Explain + apply, 2 pts): like B(ii) but with a DIFFERENT concept than B(ii). Reusing B(ii)'s concept caps C(ii) at 1.
Be fair like a real AP reader: accept any correct wording, ignore spelling, and do not award points for vague or incorrect answers. Evidence must actually support the student's claim.
